text: The Haxey Hood Games is a British folk festival. The town of Haxey in Humberside holds the mid-winter game on Twelfth Night, the last day of the old Christmas holidays. Legend dates the design to medieval times. The scarlet hood of a local noblewoman, Lady de Mowbray, flew from her head as she rode to church, and a dozen men each sprang to save it. Pleased, she gave the village a land called the Hoodland, and its field provided a hood each year for a game among twelve villagers. The twelve still play it under a leader of red-dressed figures called the gobbans. A fool opens at dawn with a speech in the town square. He closes with the cry "House against house, town against town, if you meet a man knock him down, but don't hurt him," and a fire is lit at his feet, a rite called smoking the fool. Then the King Gobban throws twelve hoods and all scramble for one. Whoever carries a hood into a village inn wins free drinks. Some scholars see memory of a human sacrifice in the rite.
objective: Document the Haxey Hood Games, the mid-winter festival of Humberside.
